title: Biggest Number From Cards
story: In a family card game, each player gets a few cards printed with whole numbers, like 7, 60 and 65. You lay your cards in a row, and the digits read left to right form one big number. Biggest number wins.
Cards can be reordered but not cut or flipped. Your cousin always leads with the highest card and keeps losing. Find the best row.
task: Write largestNumber(cards). Return, as a string, the largest number you can form by placing all the cards in some order and joining their digits.
Return it without extra leading zeros: if every card is 0, return "0", not "000". Return a string because the result can have hundreds of digits.

examples.explanation: Largest card first gives 65 60 9 7 = "656097", which loses. A leading 9 beats any 6, so 9 goes first, then 7, then 65 before 60: "976560".
Before 34, the 3 gives "334…"; after it, "343…", so 34 goes first. Between 3 and 31, "331" beats "313", so 3 goes before 31. Result "34331".

hints: Take just two cards, 3 and 31. Which order wins, and how can you tell without looking at any other card?
Glue them both ways and compare: "331" vs "313". The bigger string decides which card goes first, for any pair, even of different lengths.
A rule that orders any two cards is a comparison any sort can use. It never contradicts itself (if a beats b and b beats c, then a beats c), so sorting with it is safe.
Turn the cards into strings. Sort with the rule: a goes before b if a + b > b + a as strings. Join them. If the result starts with "0", every card was 0, so return "0".
bruteForce: Try every order of the cards and keep the biggest join. With 10 cards that is 3,628,800 orders; with 20, about 2.4 × 10¹⁸. Hopeless.
The quick guesses fail too. Sorting by numeric value puts 10 before 2 and builds "102" instead of "210". Reverse dictionary order puts "121" before "12" and builds "12112" instead of "12121".

walkthrough: You cannot rank a card on its own: whether 3 comes before 31 depends on how their digits interleave. But you can rank any pair by gluing it both ways. Give that rule to a sort, and the sort finds the best row.
Comparing glued strings is safe: a + b and b + a have the same length, so string order matches numeric order.

Why a pairwise rule gives the best row overall: if two neighbours broke the rule, swapping them would make the whole number bigger, since the digits around them stay put. The best row has no such pair, and that is what the sort guarantees.
The zero case: [0, 0, 0] sorts to "000". A leading "0" means every card is 0, so return "0".
solution.timeWhy: A comparison sort with O(n log n) comparisons; each comparison glues strings of at most 20 digits, so it is constant.
solution.spaceWhy: The list of strings and the joined result.
solution.takeaway: When the right order depends on how two items combine, define a pairwise comparator and let a standard sort do the rest. If swapping two neighbours that break the rule always improves the answer, sorting by the rule is optimal.
